lines: Morgan Patel
+1 (555) 010-4410 | morgan.patel@example.com | example.com/code/mpatel
EDUCATION
Ridgeway University | Ph.D. candidate in Statistics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2021 - Expected May 2026
Ridgeway University | B.S. in Mathematics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2016 - May 2020
EXPERIENCE
Sunrise Bakery | Assistant Store Manager | Metro City, USA | Sep 2025 - Present
- Managed opening shifts and a team of 6 bakers and cashiers, keeping the store within its weekly labour budget.
- Ran daily stock counts and supplier orders, cutting unsold bread from 12% to 7% of production.
Northpeak Capital | Quantitative Research Intern | Metro City, USA | Jun 2025 - Aug 2025
- Improved risk-adjusted returns by 35% with a cost-aware position smoother on the desk's futures signal.
- Validated the signal on 6 years of tick data with purged walk-forward splits and an embargo period, so every backtest decision used only information available at the time.
- Wrote a feature store for 120 microstructure features with point-in-time joins, which the research team reused in two later signal projects.
- Presented the signal, its capacity estimate and failure cases to the portfolio managers, who approved a small live allocation for the next quarter.
- Selected the smoother's parameters from 400 backtested configurations and reported the best one's Sharpe as the expected live Sharpe.
- Built a short-horizon order-book imbalance signal for liquid index futures that raised the desk book's Sharpe ratio from 1.1 to 1.5 over 18 months of out-of-sample backtest after costs.
Ridgeway University | Research Assistant, Statistical Learning Lab | Metro City, USA | Jun 2020 - Aug 2021
- Cut a 2,000-run Monte Carlo study from 3 days to 5 hours by running the runs in parallel with the same random seed on every worker.
- Derived a variance bound for a sparse regression estimator; my proof tightens the previous bound by a log factor and is now Section 3 of a paper under review at JASA.
- Taught weekly recitations for 60 students in graduate probability, writing 12 problem sets and earning a 4.8/5 teaching rating.
- Released an open-source R package for high-dimensional covariance estimation with shrinkage and factor models, downloaded 3,000 times in its first year.
PROJECTS
Volatility Forecasting Study | Independent Research | Python, PyTorch | Jan 2024 - Present
- Beat a HAR-RV baseline's out-of-sample QLIKE loss by 7% on 30 equity indices with a temporal convolutional model trained on realized-volatility features.
- Tested significance with Diebold-Mariano tests across the 30 indices; after a Holm correction the forecast gain held at the 5% level on 24 of them and in both crisis periods.
- Wrote up the method, robustness checks and results as a 12-page working paper, which was presented at the department's financial econometrics seminar.
Kaggle Market Prediction Competition | Team of 3 | Python | Mar 2023 - Jun 2023
- Engineered features and trained gradient-boosting models for a market prediction competition.
- Cut validation leakage by switching to time-grouped folds, which closed a 0.02 gap between local validation and leaderboard scores.
- Added 0.4 to the Sharpe ratio of a futures book with an order-book imbalance signal, tested over 18 months out of sample.
SKILLS
Programming: Python, R, PyTorch, Kafka
Methods: time-series econometircs, high-dimensional statistics, gradient boosting

items.says: The order-book imbalance result appears duplicated under Northpeak Capital and the Kaggle competition.
items.because: A reader may question whether the work was duplicated or whether the candidate's ownership and project scope are unclear.

items.says: The 35% risk-adjusted-return result is not labeled consistently with the selected backtest estimate in the same role.
items.because: The reader cannot tell whether the 35% improvement is an achieved out-of-sample result or a selected backtest estimate.

items.says: Sunrise Bakery currently receives top billing as the newest role even though the target profile is quantitative research.
items.because: Its chronological placement makes the résumé appear to be moving away from quantitative work.

items.says: The phrase 'within its weekly labour budget' does not show how far under or at budget the store finished.
items.because: The reader can see the budget target but not the scale of the result.

items.says: The bullets use broad or imprecise verbs for managing shifts, a team, and supplier orders.
items.because: The reader gets less evidence of operational ownership than the work may warrant.

items.says: The inventory practices are presented as causing the reduction in unsold bread without establishing that causal link.
items.because: Without comparable records or controls for those factors, the figures support an association rather than causal attribution.

items.says: The 35% improvement does not identify the risk-adjusted metric or its baseline.
items.because: A hiring manager cannot tell what the figure represents or reproduce the comparison from the line.

items.says: Purged walk-forward splits and an embargo do not establish that every backtest decision used only information available at the time.
items.because: These methods reduce leakage but do not guarantee point-in-time validity for all sources of leakage.

items.says: The validation method is described without stating what the validation showed.
items.because: Methodological rigor needs a concise outcome to demonstrate research value.

items.says: The feature-store adoption result is buried at the end of the bullet.
items.because: The team's reuse is the clearest evidence that the artifact mattered.

items.says: The phrase 'small live allocation' leaves the scale of the approved deployment vague.
items.because: A reader cannot distinguish a meaningful deployment decision from a token test.

items.says: The bullet delays the live-allocation outcome and uses a vague size qualifier.
items.because: The approval is the most important result, but it appears after the presentation details.

items.says: Reporting the best Sharpe from 400 backtested configurations as the expected live Sharpe is statistically invalid.
items.because: Selecting the maximum result across 400 configurations introduces multiple-testing and selection bias.

items.says: The line gives neither the selected Sharpe value nor its comparison.
items.because: Calling a configuration best is not enough to assess the result.

items.says: The parameter-selection bullet does not say what the work changed or enabled.
items.because: It reads as an internal research step rather than a contribution with a consequence.

items.says: The phrase 'the best one’s Sharpe as the expected live Sharpe' is ambiguous about both the configuration and the estimate.
items.because: The reader cannot tell what was measured or how it should be interpreted.

items.says: The bullet foregrounds the 400-configuration search before stating the result.
items.because: Leading with the configuration count makes the achievement harder to scan.

items.says: The entry's clearest quantified result appears after several implementation and validation bullets.
items.because: A scanner may not reach it; leading with the result would communicate value earlier.

items.says: Using the same random seed on every worker does not produce appropriately independent Monte Carlo replicates.
items.because: Workers generally replay identical pseudorandom sequences, which can invalidate Monte Carlo uncertainty estimates.

items.says: The phrase 'running the runs in parallel' repeats the same word and obscures the actual action.
items.because: The repetition makes the performance improvement harder to scan.

items.says: The phrase 'my proof' uses a first-person pronoun, which does not belong in a résumé bullet.
items.because: First-person wording breaks the résumé's otherwise phrase-based style.

items.says: The phrase 'by a log factor' does not identify the specific bound or term that changed.
items.because: Naming the prior and new terms would make the mathematical result assessable.

items.says: The publication-status clause delays the main mathematical result and makes the ending dense.
items.because: Reordering the result and publication status would make the achievement easier to scan.

items.says: The forecasting setup does not identify the prediction horizon or target.
items.because: The reader cannot tell what was forecast.

items.says: The claim that the gain held at the 5% level in both crisis periods is not established by the described tests across 30 indices.
items.because: Full-sample Diebold-Mariano significance does not imply significance within separate crisis-period subsets.

items.says: The phrase 'in both crisis periods' does not identify the periods tested.
items.because: A reader cannot judge the economic relevance or reproduce the crisis-period result.

items.says: The significance-testing wording is redundant, and the relationship between the 24-index result and the crisis-period result is unclear.
items.because: The ending can be read as saying either that all 24 indices held in both crises or that the crisis result is a separate claim.

items.says: The line describes authoring a paper without identifying the specific method or robustness work carried out.
items.because: A scanning reader sees documentation rather than analytical work.

items.says: The bullet uses informal wording and passive voice for the paper and seminar presentation.
items.because: The result is less direct and less evidence of ownership than it could be.

items.says: The competition project gives no result for the feature engineering and gradient-boosting work.
items.because: A hiring reader cannot see whether the models were competitive or produced a meaningful improvement.

items.says: The competition bullet repeats its setting and gives no measurable outcome.
items.because: The heading already identifies the project as a market prediction competition.

items.says: The bullet names broad methods without showing the concrete feature or modeling decision that demonstrates skill.
items.because: A specific representative detail would make the technical contribution more memorable.

items.says: Switching to time-grouped folds does not by itself establish that leakage was reduced or that the 0.02 gap was closed because of the switch.
items.because: Leakage can remain through other means, and the gap could reflect leaderboard noise or distribution shift.

items.says: The 0.02 validation-to-leaderboard gap does not identify the competition metric or what the number represents.
items.because: A reader cannot tell whether 0.02 means score points, percentage points, log loss, Sharpe, or another measure.

items.says: The result is buried in a subordinate clause after the method.
items.because: The 0.02 gap change is the bullet's measurable achievement, but a scanner may focus on the fold change and miss it.

items.says: The 0.4 Sharpe increase does not identify the starting Sharpe or the comparison baseline.
items.because: A reader cannot tell whether the change was relative to an existing strategy, a benchmark, or a no-signal version.

items.says: 'Added 0.4 to the Sharpe ratio' is less idiomatic and less precise than describing an increase by 0.4.
items.because: More direct language would make the quantitative result easier to scan.

items.says: The Kaggle entry starts as a competition project but ends with an order-book signal result that duplicates the Northpeak achievement, making the project's scope and ownership unclear.
items.because: The competition methods and the futures-book Sharpe result do not visibly belong to the same project.

items.says: The Methods skills list misspells econometrics.
items.because: The misspelling is immediately visible in a technical skills section.

items.says: Kafka is listed under Programming without evidence of Kafka use elsewhere in the résumé.
items.because: A recruiter cannot verify whether Kafka is a genuine working skill or an unsupported keyword.
